title: Pancreatic Acinar Zones
subject: Pathology
summary: Acinar zones describe the functional regions of the pancreatic exocrine tissue and their relevance in disease. Understanding zonal injury helps clinicians localise pathology, anticipate complications and choose appropriate investigations in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: The pancreas is divided into head, body and tail, each containing acinar cells that secrete digestive enzymes. Zonal injury refers to focal damage limited to one or more of these regions, often seen in pancreatitis, trauma or neoplasia.
b: Acinar zones are identified by imaging (ultrasound/CT) or intra‑operative inspection.
Clinical suspicion arises from epigastric pain radiating to the back, vomiting and elevated pancreatic enzymes.

t.b: Detects focal enlargement or hypoechoic areas in specific zones; useful where CT is unavailable.
Confirms exocrine pancreatic injury; markedly raised (>3× ULN) supports acute zonal pancreatitis.
Maps zone‑specific necrosis or fluid collections; guides management.

sections.p: Acinar zone injury is staged like acute pancreatitis using the Revised Atlanta Classification, focusing on the extent of necrosis and systemic response.
b: Mild: zone‑limited inflammation, no organ failure.
Moderately severe: transient organ failure or peripancreatic fluid collections.
Severe: persistent organ failure >48 h or extensive necrosis across multiple zones.

t.b: Assesses organ failure; a score ≥2 in any system indicates severe disease.

sections.p: In low‑resource East African hospitals, the common precipitants of zonal pancreatic injury are:
b: Gallstone obstruction (most frequent cause of focal head zone pancreatitis).
Alcohol excess (often involves body and tail).
Infectious agents: HIV‑related opportunistic infections, severe malaria, or hepatitis B‑associated cholangitis.
Trauma (blunt abdominal injury affecting tail).
Herbal or traditional medicines causing direct toxic injury.

sections.p: Patients present with acute epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, and sometimes a palpable tender mass if the tail is involved.
b: Head zone: pain may be more central, possible jaundice if bile duct compressed.
Body zone: diffuse epigastric pain, early vomiting.
Tail zone: left upper quadrant tenderness, possible splenic flexure irritation.

sections.p: Prioritise bedside tools; reserve advanced imaging for when it will change management.
b: Focused history on alcohol, gallstones, recent infections, trauma, and herbal intake.
Physical exam: epigastric tenderness, guarding, signs of peritonitis.

t.b: Answers whether there is a fluid collection or enlarged pancreas in a specific zone; if unavailable, rely on clinical assessment.
Detects organ dysfunction that defines severity.

sections.p: Complications arise from necrosis, infection or systemic inflammatory response.
b: Persistent hypotension or shock.
Respiratory failure needing oxygen or ventilation.
Renal failure (creatinine rise).
Infected pancreatic necrosis (fever, leukocytosis).

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care tailored to the affected zone.
b: Gallstone removal (ERCP or surgical exploration) for head‑zone obstruction.
Stop alcohol and give abstinence counseling.
Empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone + metronidazole) only if infection suspected; avoid routine use.
Fluid resuscitation with crystalloids (goal: maintain urine output >0.5 mL/kg/h).
Analgesia with paracetamol or low‑dose opioids; avoid NSAIDs if renal risk.

sections.p: After acute resolution, monitor for chronic changes and educate on risk reduction.
b: Repeat ultrasound at 4–6 weeks to assess for pseudocyst formation.
Vaccinate against hepatitis B and counsel on safe herbal use.
Encourage moderate alcohol intake or abstinence; treat gallstones electively if asymptomatic.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic zonal pancreatic injury:
b: Peptic ulcer perforation (sudden severe pain, free air on X‑ray).
Acute cholecystitis (right upper quadrant pain, Murphy’s sign).
Splenic infarct (left upper quadrant pain, tender spleen).

sections.p: Pitfalls in interpreting investigations:
b: Serum amylase may be normal in isolated tail necrosis; rely on imaging.
Ultrasound can miss deep pancreatic lesions in obese patients; consider CT if available.
Leukocytosis may be absent in immunocompromised HIV patients despite infection.

whenToSeekHelp: Fever >38 °C with rising white cell count after 48 h

faq.q: Why does jaundice occur with head‑zone pancreatitis?
faq.a: The inflamed head compresses the common bile duct, obstructing bilirubin flow.

faq.q: Can a normal amylase rule out pancreatic injury?
faq.a: No; focal tail necrosis may have normal enzymes, so imaging is essential if suspicion remains.

faq.q: When is surgery indicated for zonal pancreatic disease?
faq.a: When there is gallstone obstruction not amenable to endoscopic removal, infected necrosis, or uncontrolled hemorrhage.

exam: A 45‑year‑old man with epigastric pain and a history of heavy alcohol use presents in a district hospital without CT. What is your next diagnostic step and why? — Perform bedside ultrasound to look for pancreatic enlargement or fluid; it guides severity assessment when CT is unavailable.

How would you differentiate head‑zone pancreatitis from acute cholecystitis on examination? — Look for Murphy’s sign (positive in cholecystitis) versus central epigastric tenderness radiating to the back in pancreatitis.

A patient with known gallstones develops sudden severe pain and jaundice. Which zone is most likely involved and what immediate management is required? — Head zone; arrange urgent ERCP or surgical decompression to relieve biliary obstruction.
Why is routine antibiotic use discouraged in mild zonal pancreatitis? — Antibiotics do not improve outcomes and increase resistance; they are reserved for proven infection.

In a patient with HIV on antiretroviral therapy, serum amylase is normal but pain persists. What is your next step? — Obtain ultrasound or CT if possible; HIV patients may have atypical enzyme patterns.
What red‑flag laboratory change signals progression to severe disease? — Development of renal failure (creatinine rise) or persistent hypoxia despite oxygen therapy.

Explain why herbal remedies can cause pancreatic toxicity and how you would counsel a patient. — Certain herbs contain unsaturated fatty acids that precipitate enzyme activation; advise cessation and provide safer alternatives.
When is surgical debridement indicated for necrotic pancreatic zones? — When necrosis becomes infected (fever, leukocytosis) or causes persistent organ failure despite medical therapy.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: Collect focused history and perform systematic abdominal examination to localise pancreatic injury and rule out mimics.
b: History: onset, character, radiation, relation to meals, alcohol, drugs, herbal use, recent trauma, infections, gallstone symptoms
Ask about jaundice, fever, vomiting, weight loss, prior pancreatitis
Examine: inspect for pallor, jaundice, scars; palpate for epigastric tenderness, guarding, rebound
Check for Murphy’s sign (right upper quadrant pain on inspiration) – specific for cholecystitis but not exclusive to pancreas
Assess for abdominal distension, shifting dullness, fluid thrill – indicates ascites, not zone‑specific

t.b: Positive indicates acute cholecystitis; cannot distinguish pancreatic pain
Detects ascites; does not localise pancreatic zone

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Use simple, affordable tests to confirm pancreatitis, identify zone, and gauge severity; interpret indices and thresholds for management decisions.
b: If CT unavailable, rely on ultrasound and clinical severity scores; monitor fluid balance and organ function

sections.p: Apply the Revised Atlanta Classification to classify severity and guide management.
b: Hemoconcentration thresholds (47% men, 42% women) prompt aggressive fluid resuscitation

sections.p: Differentiate pancreatic zone injury from other abdominal pathologies using key distinguishing features.
b: Herbal pancreatitis – history of traditional medicine use; enzyme elevation; imaging shows focal necrosis

sections.p: A structured ladder guides clinicians from immediate stabilisation to definitive therapy, with clear triggers for escalation or referral in low‑resource settings.
b: 1. Assess airway, breathing, circulation; give oxygen if SpO2 <94% and start IV crystalloid bolus (20 mL/kg) while monitoring urine output.
2. Obtain bedside labs (amylase, lipase, full blood count, electrolytes, renal function, liver panel) and point‑of‑care glucose; if unavailable, rely on clinical dehydration signs.
3. Start analgesia with parenteral opioids (e.g., morphine) and anti‑emetics (e.g., ondansetron) to control pain and vomiting.
4. Give prophylactic proton‑pump inhibitor infusion to reduce stress gastritis; avoid routine antibiotics unless infected necrosis is suspected.
5. Identify the dominant zone (head, body, tail) by focused ultrasound; if head zone and jaundice present, arrange urgent ERCP or refer for biliary decompression.
6. For alcohol‑related body/tail disease, initiate abstinence counselling and consider early enteral nutrition via nasogastric tube if oral intake <24 h.

7. Monitor vital signs, urine output, haematocrit, BUN, and serum calcium every 6 h; escalation trigger: persistent organ failure >48 h, rising haematocrit >47% (men) or >42% (women), or new respiratory distress.
8. Refer to tertiary centre for necrosectomy or percutaneous drainage when necrotic collections become infected or cause persistent organ failure.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Key pharmacologic agents used in zonal pancreatitis have predictable adverse profiles; recognising them prevents iatrogenic harm.
b: Opioids: risk of respiratory depression and ileus; monitor respiratory rate and consider naloxone infusion if sedation deepens.
Ondansetron: may prolong QT interval; obtain baseline ECG in patients with known cardiac disease and avoid in congenital long QT.
Proton‑pump inhibitors: increase risk of Clostridioides difficile; limit duration to hospital stay and reassess need daily.
Fluids (crystalloids): over‑resuscitation can cause pulmonary oedema; stop bolus if oxygen saturation falls or lung crackles develop.
Antibiotics (if used for infected necrosis): watch for nephrotoxicity with aminoglycosides; prefer beta‑lactam/beta‑lactamase inhibitor combos and adjust for renal function.

sections.p: Complications arise from necrosis, infection, and systemic inflammatory response; early detection guides timely escalation.
b: Persistent organ failure (respiratory, renal, cardiovascular) beyond 48 h – trigger transfer to ICU or surgical centre.
Rising serum calcium >2.6 mmol/L or ionised calcium >1.3 mmol/L – suggests fat necrosis; treat with aggressive hydration and monitor cardiac rhythm.
New or worsening abdominal distension with fever – suspect infected necrotic collection; obtain CT if feasible, start broad‑spectrum antibiotics, and arrange drainage.
Hematocrit rising above 47% (men) or 42% (women) despite fluids – indicates haemoconcentration and risk of necrosis; intensify fluid resuscitation and consider early imaging.
Development of ascites with high serum‑ascites albumin gradient (>1.1 g/dL) – points to portal hypertension from severe inflammation; manage with diuretics and monitor renal function.

sections.p: Co‑morbid conditions modify presentation, laboratory interpretation, and therapeutic choices in zonal pancreatic injury.
b: HIV: amylase may be normal despite necrosis; rely on lipase and imaging; avoid nephrotoxic drugs if on tenofovir.
TB treatment (rifampicin, isoniazid) can cause hepatotoxicity, raising ALT; differentiate drug‑induced liver injury from gallstone‑related ALT rise (>150 U/L).
Severe malnutrition lowers serum albumin, exaggerating haematocrit‑based severity scores; use clinical dehydration signs instead.
Pregnancy: avoid ionising imaging unless essential; use MRI without gadolinium for zone localisation; give opioid analgesia cautiously, avoid NSAIDs after 20 weeks.
Diabetes: hyperglycaemia worsens pancreatic inflammation; monitor glucose hourly and adjust insulin; avoid high‑dose steroids.
Renal failure: limit fluid bolus to 10 mL/kg and monitor for volume overload; choose renally cleared antibiotics if needed.
Age extremes: children have higher fluid requirements per kg; elderly have reduced cardiac reserve – titrate fluids slowly and watch for delirium.

sections.p: Tailoring care to vulnerable populations ensures equitable outcomes despite limited resources.
b: Children: use weight‑based fluid resuscitation, prefer oral rehydration if tolerated, and involve paediatric surgery early for necrotic collections.
Pregnant women: prioritize maternal oxygenation, use MRI for zone assessment, give analgesia with opioids and avoid teratogenic drugs; plan delivery after stabilisation.
Elderly: start with lower fluid volumes, monitor for heart failure, use low‑dose opioids, and consider early physiotherapy to prevent deconditioning.
People with HIV: screen for opportunistic infections (CMV, Mycobacterium), use lipase as primary enzyme marker, and coordinate with antiretroviral team before adding hepatotoxic drugs.
Low‑resource settings: rely on bedside ultrasound, clinical scoring (pain, vomiting, haematocrit), and oral/NG feeding; refer only when necrosis is clinically evident or organ failure persists.

sections.p: Use these prompts to test mastery of the deep notes; each requires integration of history, exam, investigations, and management.
b: 1. A 38‑year‑old man with chronic alcohol use presents with epigastric pain radiating to the back. Which bedside sign helps differentiate body‑zone pancreatitis from perforated ulcer?
2. Explain how a haematocrit of 48% in a male patient changes your fluid‑resuscitation plan.
3. A pregnant woman at 28 weeks has suspected tail‑zone pancreatitis. Which imaging modality is safest and what information must you obtain before deciding on drainage?
4. In a patient with HIV on tenofovir, serum amylase is normal but lipase is 4 times upper limit. What is the next diagnostic step and why?
5. List three reasons why routine antibiotics are avoided in mild zonal pancreatitis.
6. A patient develops new fever and left‑upper‑quadrant tenderness on day 5. What complication is most likely and what immediate action is required?
7. How does severe malnutrition alter the interpretation of haematocrit as a severity marker?
8. Describe the sequence of fluid management for an elderly patient with head‑zone pancreatitis and borderline renal function.
9. Which acinar zone of the liver is most vulnerable to hypoxia and what cardiac condition predisposes to its injury?
10. A child with blunt abdominal trauma shows left‑sided tenderness. Outline the bedside steps to identify tail‑zone injury and the criteria for surgical referral.

facts: Revised Atlanta Classification defines severe pancreatitis as persistent organ failure >48 h or necrosis involving >30 % of pancreatic tissue.
Haemoconcentration suggesting inadequate resuscitation: haematocrit >47 % in men, >42 % in women.
Elevated ALT >150 U/L strongly points to gallstone‑related pancreatitis.
Serum amylase may be normal in HIV patients with pancreatic injury; rely on lipase and imaging.
Urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for >6 h signals impending renal failure.
CT severity index ≥7 predicts need for intensive care.
Mild pancreatitis: no organ failure, no local or systemic complications.
Moderately severe: transient organ failure or peripancreatic fluid collections.
Pancreatic necrosis most common in body and tail zones after alcohol excess.
Murphy’s sign is highly specific for acute cholecystitis but does not exclude pancreatic pain.

vivas.q: How does head‑zone pancreatitis differ from acute cholecystitis on examination?
vivas.a: Head‑zone pain is central epigastric with possible jaundice; cholecystitis shows a positive Murphy’s sign, right upper quadrant tenderness, and often a palpable gallbladder.

vivas.q: Why is routine antibiotic use discouraged in mild zonal pancreatitis?
vivas.a: Antibiotics do not reduce infection risk in sterile necrosis and increase resistance; they are reserved for proven infected necrosis.

vivas.q: Explain the significance of a normal amylase but elevated lipase in an HIV patient with abdominal pain.
vivas.a: Amylase can be normal due to HIV‑related pancreatic injury; lipase is more specific and remains elevated, confirming pancreatitis.

vivas.q: Which hepatic acinar zone is most vulnerable to injury from chronic alcohol consumption?
vivas.a: Zone 3 (centrilobular) is most susceptible to alcohol‑induced hypoxia and oxidative stress.

vivas.q: A patient presents with centrilobular necrosis after carbon tetrachloride exposure. Which acinar zone is most severely affected?
vivas.a: Zone 3, because it receives the lowest oxygen tension and highest concentration of toxic metabolites.

vivas.q: Which acinar zone receives the highest concentration of oxygenated blood?
vivas.a: Zone 1 (periportal) receives blood directly from the hepatic artery and portal vein, giving it the highest oxygen content.

vivas.q: Acinar zones are numbered 1 through 3 based on what anatomical gradient?
vivas.a: Based on the gradient of oxygen and nutrient supply from the portal triad (zone 1) to the central vein (zone 3).

vivas.q: Describe the differences in oxygenation and susceptibility to injury between Acinar Zone 1 and Zone 3 of the liver.
vivas.a: Zone 1 has high oxygen, low toxin exposure; injury causes include cholestasis. Zone 3 is hypoxic, prone to toxic injury (alcohol, CCl₄).

vivas.q: What is the main structural and functional unit of the liver and which zone is most prone to hypoxic injury?
vivas.a: The hepatic acinus; zone 3 is most prone to hypoxia, associated with conditions like congestive heart failure and toxic injury.

vivas.q: In severe right‑heart failure, which hepatic acinar zone is most affected and why?
vivas.a: Zone 3, because venous congestion lowers oxygen delivery and raises hydrostatic pressure, leading to centrilobular necrosis.

vivas.q: When is surgical debridement indicated for necrotic pancreatic zones?
vivas.a: When necrosis is infected (positive culture or gas on CT) and the patient deteriorates despite antibiotics and supportive care.

vivas.q: What is the first step in managing a patient with suspected tail‑zone pancreatitis in a district hospital without CT?
vivas.a: Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation, analgesia, and bedside ultrasound to look for peripancreatic fluid; monitor urine output and haematocrit.

vivas.q: How do you counsel a patient using herbal remedies about pancreatic toxicity?
vivas.a: Explain that certain herbs contain phytotoxins causing direct acinar injury; advise cessation and substitution with proven safe alternatives.

mcqs.q: A 52‑year‑old woman with gallstones presents with epigastric pain radiating to the back, jaundice, and ALT 210 U/L. Which pancreatic zone is most likely involved?
mcqs.e: Gallstone obstruction compresses the common bile duct near the head zone.

mcqs.q: In a patient with HIV on ART, serum amylase is normal but lipase is 4× upper limit. What is the most appropriate next step?
mcqs.e: Fluid resuscitation is first‑line; imaging is reserved for complications.

mcqs.q: Which sign is highly specific for acute cholecystitis but cannot rule out pancreatic pain?
mcqs.e: Murphy’s sign is specific for cholecystitis yet does not exclude pancreatic disease.

mcqs.q: A blunt abdominal trauma patient develops left upper quadrant tenderness and elevated lipase. Which pancreatic zone is most likely injured?
mcqs.e: Trauma commonly damages the tail zone due to its mobility.

mcqs.q: Which hepatic acinar zone is most affected by carbon tetrachloride toxicity?
mcqs.e: CCl₄ generates free radicals that damage the hypoxic zone 3.

mcqs.q: In a low‑resource setting without CT, which bedside test helps assess severity of pancreatitis?
mcqs.e: Urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h signals organ hypoperfusion and severity.

cases.v: A 62‑year‑old woman with known gallstones presents with right upper quadrant pain, jaundice, ALT 190 U/L, and lipase 3× normal. Physical exam reveals a positive Murphy’s sign and epigastric tenderness.

qs.q: Which pancreatic zone is most likely involved and why?
qs.a: Head zone, because gallstone obstruction compresses the common bile duct adjacent to the pancreatic head.

qs.q: What bedside investigation helps differentiate cholecystitis from pancreatitis here?
qs.a: Murphy’s sign (positive) suggests cholecystitis; however, elevated lipase and epigastric tenderness point to concurrent pancreatitis.

qs.q: What is the definitive management for this patient in a district hospital?
qs.a: Stabilize with fluids and analgesia, then arrange urgent ERCP or surgical biliary decompression; antibiotics only if infection suspected.

mistakes: Assuming normal amylase rules out pancreatitis in HIV patients; always check lipase and imaging.
Prescribing antibiotics for all cases of mild pancreatitis; they are only for proven infection.
Relying on Murphy’s sign to exclude pancreatic disease; it is specific for cholecystitis but does not rule out pancreatitis.
Neglecting urine output monitoring when haematocrit is unavailable; output is a key severity marker.
Confusing hepatic acinar zones with pancreatic zones; keep the two organ systems distinct in answers.
Failing to mention the need for referral when necrosis is extensive or organ failure persists.
Over‑interpreting ALT elevation without considering gallstone pancreatitis; ALT >150 U/L is a strong clue.
